definition: The cards you bring to play with. In Standard, a deck has at least 60 cards.
In Magic's story, you, the player, are a planeswalker: a powerful wizard. There's also a card type with the same name, which you'll meet later.
A card you're casting. It becomes a spell while it waits to take effect. Lands are never spells: you play them, you don't cast them.
How much life a player has. Each player starts with 20 in a normal game. Damage lowers it. At 0 or less, that player loses.
The player you're playing against.
Your deck, once the game has started. It sits face down, and you draw cards from the top of it.
A marker some cards give to a player. A player with 10 or more poison counters loses the game.
The energy you spend to cast spells. Lands make most of it. Each mana is white, blue, black, red, green, or colourless.
A card you play (not cast) to make mana. You may play one land per turn, during your main phase.
Turn a card sideways to show you've used it, for example to make mana or to attack. It stays tapped until it untaps.
Turn a tapped card back upright. All your cards untap at the start of each of your turns.
The symbols in a card's top-right corner. They show what mana you must pay to cast it.
The total amount of mana in a card's cost. A card costing one generic and one red mana has a mana value of 2.
A number in a mana cost, shown in a grey circle. You can pay it with mana of any colour.
Where mana waits after you make it. Unused mana empties out at the end of each step and phase, so spend it right away.
What kind of card something is, shown on its type line: land, creature, instant, sorcery, artifact, enchantment, planeswalker or battle.
A card or token on the battlefield. Lands, creatures, artifacts, enchantments and planeswalkers become permanents. Instants and sorceries never do.
A permanent that can attack and block. It has power (the damage it deals) and toughness (how much damage destroys it).
A spell you can cast almost any time, even during your opponent's turn. It does its thing, then goes to the graveyard.
A spell you can cast only during your own main phase, when nothing is waiting on the stack. Then it goes to the graveyard.
A permanent that's a magical object. Many artifacts are colourless, so any deck can use them.
A permanent with an ongoing magical effect. An Aura is an enchantment that attaches to something.
The line in the middle of a card, under the picture. It shows the card type, for example Creature, and often a subtype like Dog.
The two numbers in a creature's corner, like 2/1. Power is the damage it deals. Toughness is how much damage destroys it in one turn.
A word on a card that's short for a rule, like Flying or Haste.
A place where cards can be during a game: library, hand, battlefield, graveyard, stack, exile and command.
The cards you're holding. Your opponent can't see them. You start the game with seven.
The shared play area in front of both players, where permanents are. Cards here stay until something removes them.
Your face-up discard pile. Used instants and sorceries, destroyed creatures and discarded cards go here.
A zone for cards removed from the game. Exiled cards usually never come back.
Where spells and abilities wait before they happen. The last thing added happens first.
Shuffling away your opening hand to draw a new seven. For each mulligan, you then put one card from that hand on the bottom of your library.
One part of a turn. Every turn has five phases: beginning, first main, combat, second main and ending.
A smaller part inside a phase. For example, the beginning phase has three steps: untap, upkeep and draw.
The part of your turn where you can play a land and cast creatures, sorceries, artifacts, enchantments and planeswalkers. Each turn has two.
Sending your untapped creatures at your opponent (or one of their planeswalkers) during combat. Attacking taps a creature, unless it has Vigilance.
Putting your untapped creature in front of an attacking creature. They deal damage to each other instead of to you.
The everyday name for this rule: a creature can't attack, or use an ability with the tap symbol, until you've controlled it since the start of your turn.
Damage to a player makes them lose that much life. Damage to a creature stays marked on it until the end of the turn.
A creature with Flying can only be blocked by creatures with Flying or Reach.
A creature with Haste can attack, and use tap abilities, the turn it arrives. It ignores summoning sickness.
When a creature with Trample is blocked, damage beyond what's needed to destroy the blockers goes through to the player.
Any amount of damage from a creature with Deathtouch destroys the creature it hits.
A creature with First strike deals its combat damage before creatures without it.
Permission to cast a spell or use an ability. Players pass it back and forth. When everyone passes in a row, the top of the stack happens.
When a spell or ability actually happens. It leaves the stack and does what it says.
To cancel a spell while it waits on the stack. A countered spell does nothing and goes to its owner's graveyard.
A set of rules for which cards and decks you may use. The core rules of the game are the same in every format.
A one-against-one format that uses only recent sets. Decks have at least 60 cards and at most four copies of any card except basic lands.
A format, usually for four players. Each deck has exactly 100 cards, only one copy of each except basic lands, and a legendary creature leading it.
All the mana symbols on a card, including in its rules text. In Commander, every card in your deck must fit your commander's colour identity.
The idea that each of the five colours has its own personality and its own usual abilities. It guides how cards are designed. It's a design habit, not a game rule.
Damage dealt by a creature with Lifelink also makes its controller gain that much life.
A creature with Vigilance doesn't tap when it attacks, so it can still block on your opponent's turn.
A creature with Reach can block creatures with Flying.
A deck with only one copy of each card, except basic lands. Commander decks are singleton.
A supertype on a card's type line. A legendary creature can be your commander. You can't control two legendary permanents with the same name at once.
The zone where your commander sits at the start of a Commander game, and where it can return when it would leave the battlefield.
The everyday name for the extra cost: casting your commander from the command zone costs {2} more for each time you've already cast it from there.
Combat damage dealt to a player by one commander over the whole game. At 21 or more from the same commander, that player loses.
The everyday name for the chat before a casual game, where the table agrees what kind of game it wants and any house rules. Not a printed rule.
One of five power levels Wizards describes for Commander decks, from 1 (Exhibition) to 5 (cEDH). Saying your bracket helps a table match decks.
Formats where you build your deck in advance from cards you own: at least 60 cards, no more than four of each except basic lands.
Formats where you build a deck at the event from booster packs you open: at least 40 cards, and you may use every copy you opened.
A sealed pack of random cards from one set. Limited events are played with the cards opened from boosters.
A Limited format: players open packs, pick one card each and pass the rest around the table, then build 40-card decks from their picks.
A Limited format: each player opens six booster packs and builds a 40-card deck from them. No passing.
A casual Sealed event run by shops the weekend before a new set is released. A good first event.
When the oldest sets leave the Standard format each year, so the card pool stays recent. Pioneer, Modern and Commander don't rotate.
How scarce a card is in packs, shown by its set symbol's colour: common (black), uncommon (silver), rare (gold), mythic rare (orange-red).
Cards that give you extra mana beyond one land a turn: mana rocks, creatures that tap for mana, or spells that fetch lands.
Getting more cards than your opponents over the game, usually by drawing extra cards. Drawing a card and then discarding one doesn't count.
A spell or ability that gets rid of an opponent's card: destroy, exile, bounce it to hand, or counter it.
A spell that destroys or exiles every creature (or every permanent of a kind) at once, resetting the table.
How many of your cards cost 1, 2, 3, 4 and so on. A good curve has lots of cheap cards and only a few expensive ones.
When cards make each other better. Counted as points of contact: how many of the deck's interests a card touches.
A card that can actually end the game from a normal board, such as a big evasive creature or a spell that drains every opponent.
A card on Wizards' list of unusually powerful Commander cards. One in a deck makes it at least Bracket 3; four or more, Bracket 4. The list is updated by Wizards.
